Its Empire State Plaza is a sprawling modernist government complex.

Q1425428.name: Newcastle upon Tyne
facts: Its Tyne Bridge and swing bridges cross the river; the Angel of the North stands nearby.
Locals are known as Geordies, and its football club plays at St James' Park.
Hadrian's Wall began just east of here, and coal shipping made it famous.

Q42308.name: Kharkiv
facts: Its Freedom Square is one of the largest city squares in Europe.
The constructivist Derzhprom building was among the first Soviet skyscrapers.
Lies close to the Russian border and was heavily bombarded after 2022.

Q12994.name: Bruges
facts: Its canals and medieval centre earned it the nickname 'Venice of the North'.
Famous for its belfry tower, lace and chocolate; a 2008 Colin Farrell hitman film is named after it.
Was a major medieval trading hub until its access to the North Sea silted up.

Q546.name: Trieste
facts: A port at the head of the Adriatic, wedged against the Slovenian border.
James Joyce lived here and wrote much of Ulysses in the city.
Famous for coffee culture, home of illy, and the cliffside Miramare Castle.

Q1844.name: Vaduz
facts: A small capital on the Rhine, with a castle on the hillside above that is home to the reigning prince.
Its neighbours across the river and over the mountains are Switzerland and Austria.
Has a famous postage stamp museum and sits in one of the world's smallest countries.

Q36433.name: Porto
facts: Gave its name to port wine, aged in cellars across the Douro River in Vila Nova de Gaia.
Famous for the Dom Luís I iron bridge and the francesinha sandwich.
J.K. Rowling taught English here in the early 1990s.

Q10717.name: Georgetown
facts: Lies on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Demerara River, much of it below sea level.
Nicknamed the 'Garden City of the Caribbean', it is protected by a long seawall.
Its St. George's Cathedral is one of the tallest wooden churches in the world.

Q18575.name: Tucson
facts: Lies in the Sonoran Desert, flanked by the two halves of Saguaro National Park.
Home to a huge aircraft 'boneyard' at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base.
The first city in its country named a UNESCO City of Gastronomy, famous for Sonoran hot dogs.

Q430776.name: Nazareth
facts: Jesus grew up here according to the Gospels.
Home to the Basilica of the Annunciation, the largest church in the Middle East.
Sits in the hills of Lower Galilee, not far from the Sea of Galilee.

Q43199.name: Omaha
facts: Home to Warren Buffett and his company Berkshire Hathaway.
Hosts the College World Series of baseball every June.
Lies on the Missouri River and is known for its steaks and Henry Doorly Zoo.

Q648.name: Lille
facts: Near the Belgian border, it hosts one of Europe's biggest flea markets each September.
Charles de Gaulle was born here.
Famous for waffles from Méert and its Grand Place surrounded by Flemish-style buildings.

Q42462.name: York
facts: Founded by the Romans as Eboracum, it was later the Viking city of Jorvik.
Its Gothic Minster is one of the largest cathedrals in northern Europe.
Its medieval walls and the Shambles, a crooked medieval street, draw crowds.

Q16558.name: Fort Worth
facts: Nicknamed 'Cowtown', with twice-daily cattle drives in its Stockyards district.
Sits at the western end of a metroplex shared with Dallas.
Home to the Kimbell Art Museum, designed by Louis Kahn.

Q35997.name: İzmir
facts: Known in antiquity as Smyrna, it is a port on a deep gulf of the Aegean.
Homer is traditionally said to have been born here.
The ruins of ancient Ephesus lie a short drive to the south.

Q1663.name: Split
facts: Its old town grew inside the palace of the Roman emperor Diocletian.
An Adriatic port with ferries to islands such as Brač and Hvar.
Its Hajduk football club and seafront Riva promenade are local icons.

Q39178.name: Port of Spain
facts: Hosts one of the world's biggest Carnival celebrations before Lent.
The steelpan drum was invented on the island it sits on.
Lies on the Gulf of Paria, just off the coast of Venezuela.

Q49255.name: Tampa
facts: Lies on a large bay on the Gulf of Mexico, linked to St. Petersburg by causeways.
Its Ybor City district was famous for hand-rolled cigars.
Home to the Buccaneers NFL team and the Busch Gardens theme park.

Q1960.name: Dar es Salaam
facts: Its name comes from Arabic for 'Abode of Peace'.
A major Indian Ocean port, with ferries running to Zanzibar.
Was the national capital until the government moved to Dodoma.

Q11568.name: Darwin
facts: Named after the naturalist who wrote On the Origin of Species, though he never visited it.
Destroyed by Cyclone Tracy on Christmas Day 1974, and bombed by Japan in 1942.
Gateway to Kakadu National Park, famous for saltwater crocodiles and monsoon storms.

Q1555.name: Guatemala City
facts: Sits in a highland valley surrounded by volcanoes, including Pacaya and Agua.
Became the capital after earthquakes ruined the old capital, Antigua.
In 2010 a huge sinkhole opened up in the middle of the city.

Q33405.name: Little Rock
facts: Nine Black students desegregated its Central High School in 1957 under armed escort.
Home to the Clinton Presidential Center.
Named after a small rock formation on a river bank used as a landmark by early travellers.

Q24879.name: Bremen
facts: The Grimm tale of four animals who set off to become town musicians is named after it.
Its Roland statue and Town Hall on the market square are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
A Hanseatic port on the Weser River, and Beck's beer is brewed here.

Q158119.name: Ramallah
facts: Its name means 'God's Height', and it sits in the hills just north of Jerusalem.
Yasser Arafat's mausoleum is in the Muqata'a compound here.
Was historically a Christian town and a summer retreat for its cool hill climate.

Q16562.name: El Paso
facts: Sits on the Rio Grande directly across from Ciudad Juárez.
Its name means 'the pass', referring to a route through the mountains.
The Franklin Mountains run through it; it is home to Fort Bliss.

Q42956.name: Harbin
facts: Famous for its winter Ice and Snow Festival with giant illuminated ice sculptures.
Founded as a railway town, it has Russian-style buildings such as St. Sophia Cathedral.
Sits on the Songhua River and is nicknamed the 'Ice City'.

Q5687.name: Jericho
facts: In the Bible, its walls came tumbling down when Joshua's army blew trumpets.
Lies below sea level near the Dead Sea, making it the lowest city in the world.
Considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities, with remains over 10,000 years old.

Q13375.name: Pisa
facts: Home to the famous Leaning Tower, the bell tower of its cathedral.
Galileo was born here and is said to have dropped balls from the tower.
Sits on the Arno River just before it reaches the Ligurian Sea.

Q28218.name: Baton Rouge
facts: Its name means 'red stick', after a pole marking a boundary seen by French explorers.
Sits on the Mississippi River and has the tallest state capitol building in the nation.
Its big state university's Tigers football team keeps a live tiger mascot on campus.

Q2211.name: Malmö
facts: Linked to Copenhagen across the Öresund by a bridge and tunnel.
Its twisting Turning Torso was the first twisted skyscraper in the world.
Zlatan Ibrahimović grew up here; it hosted the Eurovision Song Contest in 2013 and 2024.

Q13670.name: Syracuse
facts: Archimedes was born here and died during the Roman siege.
Its old town is on Ortygia, an island in the Ionian Sea.
Has a huge Greek theatre and a cave called the Ear of Dionysius.

Q41621.name: Haifa
facts: Its Bahá'í Gardens cascade down Mount Carmel in terraces.
A Mediterranean port on a large bay, home to the Technion technology university.
Has a short underground funicular railway called the Carmelit.

Q13364.name: Ravenna
facts: Famous for glittering early Christian mosaics in churches like San Vitale.
Was the capital of the Western Roman Empire in its final decades.
Dante is buried here after dying in exile.

Q4970.name: Hangzhou
facts: Its West Lake is a famous scenic lake with causeways and pagodas.
The southern end of the Grand Canal, and home of Alibaba.
Famous for Longjing (Dragon Well) green tea and for silk.

Q43668.name: Louisville
facts: Churchill Downs hosts the famous horse race run on the first Saturday in May.
Muhammad Ali was born and buried here.
Sits on the Ohio River and is famous for its wooden baseball bats.

Q131694.name: Aden
facts: Its old district sits in the crater of an extinct volcano.
A strategic port near the mouth of the Red Sea, held by Britain for over a century.
Gives its name to the gulf it sits on.

Q26793.name: Bergen
facts: Its colourful wooden Hanseatic wharf, Bryggen, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Surrounded by seven mountains and known as one of Europe's rainiest cities.
Composer Edvard Grieg was born here; it is a gateway to the western fjords.

Q1538.name: Pune
facts: Formerly called Poona, it sits on the Deccan Plateau east of Mumbai.
Its Shaniwar Wada fort was the seat of the Maratha Peshwas.
Badminton in its modern form is said to have been formalised by British officers here.

Q38234.name: Nagasaki
facts: Hit by the second atomic bomb on 9 August 1945.
For two centuries its Dejima island was the country's only window to European trade.
Castella sponge cake is a famous local speciality, introduced by Portuguese traders.

Q42053.name: Isfahan
facts: An old saying called it 'half the world' for its splendour.
Famous for Safavid mosques, tiled domes and the Si-o-se-pol bridge.
The Zayandeh River flows through it.

Q37995.name: Yangon
facts: Home to the golden Shwedagon Pagoda.
Formerly known as Rangoon, it was the capital until 2005.
Lies near the Andaman Sea where several rivers meet.

Q37043.name: Tallahassee
facts: Its university's football team, the Seminoles, is a college football powerhouse.
Chosen as capital because it lay halfway between St. Augustine and Pensacola.
Lies in the Panhandle near the Georgia border, with canopy roads under oaks.

Q29364.name: Montgomery
facts: Rosa Parks' arrest here in 1955 sparked a year-long bus boycott.
Martin Luther King Jr. was a pastor at a church here.
The 1965 voting rights march from Selma ended here.

Q1711.name: Potsdam
facts: Home to Sanssouci, the rococo palace of Frederick the Great.
Allied leaders met at its Cecilienhof Palace in 1945 to settle the post-war order in Europe.
Lies just southwest of Berlin, linked by the Glienicke Bridge of spy swap fame.

Q28848.name: Saint Paul
facts: Forms the Twin Cities with Minneapolis across the Mississippi River.
F. Scott Fitzgerald was born here.
Hosts a famous Winter Carnival with ice palaces.

Q33486.name: Hartford
facts: Nicknamed the 'Insurance Capital of the World'.
Mark Twain wrote Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn while living here.
Harriet Beecher Stowe lived next door to Mark Twain here.

Q1296.name: Ghent
facts: Home to the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb altarpiece by the van Eyck brothers.
Its medieval Gravensteen castle sits in the city centre.
Holds a huge 10-day street festival each July and has many vegetarian restaurants.

Q43788.name: Madison
facts: Sits on an isthmus between Lakes Mendota and Monona.
Named after James Madison, fourth president and father of the Constitution.
Home to a large flagship state university and a famous farmers' market around the capitol.

Q5582862.name: Cusco
facts: Was the capital of the Inca Empire.
Gateway to Machu Picchu and the Sacred Valley.
Inca stonework, like the famous 12-angled stone, survives in its streets.

Q42448.name: Sheffield
facts: Famous for steel and stainless steel, invented here in 1913.
Home to the world's oldest football club, founded in 1857.
The film The Full Monty was set here.

Q25395.name: Newark
facts: Home to a major airport serving New York City.
Whitney Houston was born here.
Sits on the Passaic River, and the Ironbound district is famous for Portuguese food.

Q30974.name: Rouen
facts: Joan of Arc was burned at the stake here in 1431.
Monet painted its Gothic cathedral facade dozens of times.
Lies on the Seine between Paris and the English Channel.

Q79990.name: Christchurch
facts: Hit by devastating earthquakes in 2010 and 2011.
Has a temporary cathedral made of cardboard tubes.
The Avon River winds through it, with punting past its Botanic Gardens.

Q2966.name: Heidelberg
facts: Home to the country's oldest university, founded in 1386.
Its castle ruins overlook the Neckar River.
Mark Twain wrote about it, and its Old Bridge is famous.

Q40191.name: Hobart
facts: Sits beneath Mount Wellington on the Derwent River estuary.
A famous yacht race from Sydney finishes here around New Year.
Home to MONA, the Museum of Old and New Art.

Q47916.name: Lucknow
facts: Famous for its Nawabi cuisine, especially kebabs and biryani.
Its Bara Imambara includes a maze called the Bhool Bhulaiya.
Sits on the Gomti River and was a center of the 1857 rebellion.

Q42800.name: Belo Horizonte
facts: Planned in the 1890s, surrounded by mountains rich in iron ore.
Its Pampulha complex was designed by Oscar Niemeyer.
The Mineirão stadium hosted the 7-1 World Cup semi-final in 2014.

Q40236.name: Manaus
facts: Its grand Teatro Amazonas opera house was built during the rubber boom.
Lies near the Meeting of Waters, where the dark Rio Negro meets the Solimões.
Deep in the Amazon rainforest, it is reachable mostly by river or air.

Q79848.name: Southampton
facts: The Titanic set sail from here in 1912.
The Mayflower departed from here before Plymouth.
Sits on an estuary facing the Isle of Wight.

Q81033.name: Monterrey
facts: Overlooked by the saddle-shaped Cerro de la Silla mountain.
An industrial hub famous for steel and cabrito (roasted kid goat).
Its Macroplaza is one of the world's largest city squares.

Q28198.name: Jackson
facts: Named after Andrew Jackson, the seventh president.
Eudora Welty lived and wrote here.
Sits on the Pearl River and was so burned in 1863 it was nicknamed 'Chimneyville'.

Q3688.name: Nouakchott
facts: Built from scratch in the late 1950s as the capital.
Lies on the Atlantic coast at the edge of the Sahara, threatened by sand dunes.
Its fish market on the beach is famous for colourful pirogue boats.

Q43070.name: Donetsk
facts: Founded by Welsh industrialist John Hughes as Yuzovka.
A coal mining center in the Donbas region.
Its football club Shakhtar is one of the country's most successful.

Q40738.name: Bursa
facts: Was the first capital of the Ottoman Empire.
Famous for İskender kebab, invented here.
Sits at the foot of Mount Uludağ, a ski resort.

Q5468.name: Durban
facts: Famous for bunny chow, a curry served in a hollowed-out loaf.
A major Indian Ocean port with warm-water surfing beaches.
Has a large Indian community; Gandhi lived nearby.

Q2132.name: Victoria
facts: Sits on the southern tip of Vancouver Island.
Famous for afternoon tea at the Empress Hotel.
Its Butchart Gardens are world-famous.

Q126148.name: Tangier
facts: Faces Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar.
Was an international zone that attracted writers like William Burroughs.
Ibn Battuta, the medieval traveler, was born here.

Q9270.name: Thimphu
facts: One of the only capitals in the world without traffic lights.
Lies in a Himalayan valley on the Wang Chhu river.
Overlooked by a giant Buddha Dordenma statue.

Q79867.name: Birmingham
facts: Its 16th Street Baptist Church was bombed in 1963, killing four girls.
Nicknamed the 'Magic City' for its rapid growth as a steel town.
Its giant iron statue of Vulcan overlooks the city from Red Mountain.

Q3238.name: Tegucigalpa
facts: Its Toncontín airport is famous for one of the world's most difficult approaches.
Overlooked by a giant statue of Christ on El Picacho hill.
Twin city with Comayagüela, across the Choluteca River.

Q39042.name: Cheyenne
facts: Hosts Frontier Days, one of the world's largest outdoor rodeos.
Founded as a stop on the Union Pacific railroad.
Named after an Indigenous nation of the Great Plains.

Q41158.name: Cortina d'Ampezzo
facts: A glamorous ski resort ringed by the jagged peaks of the Dolomites.
Hosted the 1956 Winter Olympics and co-hosted the 2026 Games with Milan.
Roger Moore's James Bond skied and fought here in For Your Eyes Only.

Q3919.name: Gaborone
facts: Named after a 19th-century chief of the Batlokwa people, who settled here by the river.
Setting of Alexander McCall Smith's novels The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency.
Sits on the Notwane River just a few kilometres from the South African border.

Q657461.name: Cartagena
facts: A walled colonial port on the Caribbean, guarded by the huge Castillo San Felipe de Barajas.
Gabriel García Márquez lived here and drew on its streets for Love in the Time of Cholera.
Its walls were built against pirates; Francis Drake captured and ransomed the city in 1586.

Q3889.name: Maputo
facts: Known as Lourenço Marques until independence from Portugal in 1975.
Lies on a large bay of the Indian Ocean, close to the borders of Eswatini and South Africa.
Birthplace of marrabenta, a fast dance music that mixes local rhythms with guitar.

Q41262.name: Nottingham
facts: Legendary home of Robin Hood's enemy the Sheriff, with Sherwood Forest just to the north.
Its football club Forest won the European Cup twice in a row, in 1979 and 1980.
Boots the chemist and Raleigh bicycles were both founded here, on the River Trent.

Q43048.name: Rhodes
facts: Its harbour was once straddled, legend says, by the Colossus, one of the Seven Wonders.
The Knights Hospitaller built its walled medieval old town and the Palace of the Grand Master.
An island in the Aegean's Dodecanese chain, just off the coast of Turkey.

Q36947.name: Salvador
facts: The colony's first capital, ruling the Portuguese New World until 1763.
The Elevador Lacerda lifts people between its upper and lower towns above the Bay of All Saints.
A heartland of Afro-diasporic culture, capoeira and a huge street Carnival in the Pelourinho.

Q3110.name: San Salvador
facts: Sits in the 'Valley of the Hammocks' beneath the Quetzaltepec volcano, and is often shaken by quakes.
Archbishop Óscar Romero, now a saint, was shot here while saying Mass in 1980.
Pupusas, thick stuffed corn tortillas, are the beloved street food here.

Q891.name: Nizhny Novgorod
facts: Built where the Oka River flows into the Volga, crowned by a red-brick kremlin.
Called Gorky for decades after the writer Maxim Gorky, who was born here.
Physicist Andrei Sakharov was exiled to this then-closed city in the 1980s.

Q36647.name: Cork
facts: Built on islands in the River Lee; its name comes from an old word for 'marsh'.
The Blarney Stone, kissed for the gift of the gab, is in a castle just outside the city.
Nearby Cobh, then Queenstown, was the Titanic's last port of call in 1912.

Q1863.name: Andorra la Vella
facts: The highest capital city in Europe, at about 1,000 m up in the Pyrenees.
A duty-free shopping magnet squeezed into a valley between France and Spain.
Its country's heads of state are two co-princes: a Catalan bishop and the president of France.

Q44989.name: Tulsa
facts: Once called the 'Oil Capital of the World'; a giant Golden Driller statue celebrates it.
In 1921 a white mob destroyed its prosperous Greenwood district, known as Black Wall Street.
Historic Route 66 runs through it, and it sits on the Arkansas River.

Q1735.name: Innsbruck
facts: Its name means 'bridge over the Inn', and the Alps rise straight up behind the old town.
Hosted the Winter Olympics twice, in 1964 and 1976.
Famous for the Goldenes Dachl, a balcony roof covered in gilded copper tiles.

Q14960.name: Brno
facts: Gregor Mendel founded genetics by breeding pea plants in the abbey garden here.
Mies van der Rohe's modernist Villa Tugendhat is a UNESCO World Heritage Site here.
The Bren light machine gun was named after this city and Enfield.

Q3808.name: Yaoundé
facts: A capital spread across seven hills in the forested interior, inland from the Atlantic coast.
Football legend Roger Milla, star of the 1990 World Cup, was born here.
Founded as a German trading and military post in the late 1880s.

Q49266.name: Wichita
facts: Nicknamed the 'Air Capital of the World' as home to Cessna, Beechcraft and Learjet.
Pizza Hut was founded here in 1958, and White Castle burgers in 1921.
The Keeper of the Plains statue stands where the Arkansas and Little Arkansas rivers meet.

Q23311.name: City of London
facts: Known as the Square Mile, it covers the old Roman town of Londinium on the Thames.
Home to St Paul's Cathedral, the nation's central bank and the skyscraper nicknamed the Gherkin.
The Great Fire of 1666 started in a bakery on Pudding Lane here.

Q807.name: Lausanne
facts: The International Olympic Committee has its headquarters and an Olympic Museum here.
Climbs steeply from the shore of Lake Geneva, facing the Alps across the water.
A night watchman still calls out the hours from its cathedral tower.

Q36405.name: Aberdeen
facts: Nicknamed the Granite City for its sparkling grey stone buildings.
Europe's offshore oil capital, serving the North Sea rigs.
Lies between the mouths of the rivers Dee and Don; Balmoral Castle is up the Dee valley.

Q3070.name: San José
facts: Lies in a high Central Valley ringed by volcanoes such as Irazú and Poás.
Its ornate National Theatre was paid for with a tax on coffee exports.
A museum under its main plaza holds a big hoard of pre-Columbian gold.

Q47265.name: Palo Alto
facts: Its Spanish name means 'tall stick', after a lone redwood that still stands by the creek.
A garage here where Hewlett and Packard started in 1939 is called the birthplace of Silicon Valley.
Steve Jobs lived here, and Stanford University sits right next door.

Q41876.name: Reims
facts: For centuries kings were crowned in its Gothic cathedral, where Clovis was baptised.
Champagne houses like Veuve Clicquot and Taittinger age their bubbly in chalk cellars here.
Germany signed its unconditional surrender here on 7 May 1945, at Eisenhower's headquarters.

Q6441.name: Montpellier
facts: Home to one of the oldest medical schools still in operation, where Rabelais studied.
A university city a few kilometres inland from the Mediterranean.
Its Antigone district is a giant neoclassical housing estate by architect Ricardo Bofill.

Q121157.name: Mashhad
facts: Grew up around the shrine of Imam Reza, one of the largest mosque complexes in the world.
A centre of the saffron trade, near the borders of Turkmenistan and Afghanistan.
The poet Ferdowsi, author of the Shahnameh, is buried at nearby Tus.

Q1295.name: Dortmund
facts: Its football club Borussia plays before the 'Yellow Wall', a huge standing terrace.
A former coal and steel city on the eastern edge of the Ruhr.
Gave its name to a pale lager style known as Export.

Q3832.name: Bangui
facts: Lies on the Ubangi River, which forms the border with DR Congo opposite the town of Zongo.
Jean-Bédel Bokassa crowned himself emperor here in a lavish ceremony in 1977.
Pope Francis opened the 2015 Jubilee's first Holy Door in its cathedral.

Q268.name: Poznań
facts: Two mechanical goats butt heads above its town hall clock every day at noon.
Known for St. Martin's croissants, filled with white poppy seed, eaten on 11 November.
Lies on the Warta River, midway between Berlin and Warsaw.

Q52535.name: Rosario
facts: Lionel Messi was born here, and so was Che Guevara.
A big river port on the west bank of the Paraná.
The National Flag Memorial marks where Manuel Belgrano first raised the national flag in 1812.

Q6397.name: Avignon
facts: The popes lived here in the 14th century; their vast Gothic palace still dominates the town.
Its broken bridge, the Pont Saint-Bénézet, is the subject of a famous children's song.
A walled town on the Rhône that hosts a major theatre festival every July.

Q5764.name: Bukhara
facts: A Silk Road oasis where Genghis Khan is said to have spared the towering Kalyan Minaret.
The great physician Avicenna was born in a village nearby around 980.
Its rulers lived in the Ark, a massive fortress, and its rugs are known worldwide.

Q225641.name: Mombasa
facts: Fort Jesus was built here by the Portuguese in the 1590s to guard the harbour.
An island city on the Indian Ocean coast, with a Swahili old town.
Start of the 'Lunatic Express', the colonial railway built inland toward Lake Victoria.

Q617.name: Padua
facts: Giotto covered the walls of its Scrovegni Chapel with famous frescoes.
Galileo taught at its university, and its botanical garden from 1545 is the world's oldest.
Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew is set here, about 40 km west of Venice.

Q26600.name: Fukuoka
facts: Hakata tonkotsu ramen comes from here; open-air yatai food stalls line its streets at night.
A Mongol invasion fleet landing in its bay in 1281 was destroyed by the 'kamikaze' divine wind.
Lies on the north coast of Kyushu, closer to Busan than to Tokyo.

Q80053.name: Tabriz
facts: Its vast covered bazaar is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Famous for hand-knotted carpets, and for Shams, the wandering mystic who inspired Rumi.
Lies in the northwest near the salt lake Urmia, under the volcano Mount Sahand.

Q2751.name: Siena
facts: Horses race bareback around its shell-shaped Piazza del Campo in the Palio, twice a year.
The earth pigment burnt sienna takes its name from here.
Banca Monte dei Paschi, founded here in 1472, is called the world's oldest surviving bank.

Q38453.name: Columbia
facts: Sherman's Union army captured it in 1865 and much of the city burned.
The Broad and Saluda rivers meet here to form the Congaree.
Hootie & the Blowfish formed as students at its university, home of the Gamecocks.

Q6487.name: Antalya
facts: The main hub of the Turquoise Coast, backed by the Taurus Mountains.
Its Kaleiçi old town is entered through Hadrian's Gate, built for the Roman emperor in 130 AD.
Waterfalls from the Düden River plunge straight off cliffs into the Mediterranean here.

Q1947.name: Juba
facts: Lies on the White Nile.
Became the capital of the world's newest country in 2011.
The Nile flows north from here into the Sudd, one of the world's largest swamps.

Q3780.name: Freetown
facts: Founded in 1792 for freed slaves, many arriving from Nova Scotia.
A giant Cotton Tree in its centre was a symbol of freedom for over two centuries until it fell in 2023.
Fourah Bay College, founded here in 1827, is the oldest Western-style university in West Africa.

Q49258.name: Colorado Springs
facts: Sits at the foot of Pikes Peak, whose view inspired the song America the Beautiful.
Home to the Air Force Academy and the Olympic and Paralympic Training Center.
NORAD's bunker is dug into Cheyenne Mountain, and red rocks rise in the Garden of the Gods.

Q47716.name: Charleston
facts: The Civil War's first shots were fired on Fort Sumter in its harbour in 1861.
Locals joke the Ashley and Cooper rivers meet here to form the Atlantic Ocean.
Gave its name to a 1920s dance craze, and is known for pastel Rainbow Row houses.

Q36168.name: Bridgetown
facts: Rihanna grew up here, on the island she calls home.
George Washington stayed here in 1751, his only trip abroad.
Has a Trafalgar Square with a Nelson statue older than London's.

Q8969.name: Cancun
facts: A planned resort built from scratch in the 1970s on a strip of sand shaped like a '7'.
On the Caribbean tip of the Yucatán Peninsula, a jumping-off point for Chichén Itzá.
Has an underwater museum of hundreds of sculptures that grow into artificial reef.

Q43301.name: Fresno
facts: Its name means 'ash tree' and it lies in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley.
Gateway to Yosemite, Sequoia and Kings Canyon national parks.
Writer William Saroyan was born here; it is a famed raisin capital.

Q6225.name: Coventry
facts: Lady Godiva is said to have ridden naked through its streets in protest at taxes.
Its cathedral was bombed in 1940; the new one by Basil Spence stands beside the ruins.
Birthplace of the 2 Tone ska music of The Specials, and an old car-making centre.

Q131491.name: Brighton
facts: George IV built the onion-domed Royal Pavilion at this seaside resort.
Mods and rockers clashed on its beach in the 1960s, as shown in the film Quadrophenia.
Has a pebble beach, a Palace Pier on the Channel, and the ruins of the West Pier.

Q1720.name: Mainz
facts: Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type here around 1450.
Sits on the Rhine opposite the mouth of the Main.
BioNTech developed its COVID-19 vaccine here; the city also has a famous carnival.

Q83065.name: Leicester
facts: The bones of King Richard III were found under a car park here in 2012.
Its football club, the Foxes, won the Premier League in 2016 against 5000-1 odds.
Walkers crisps are made here, and its Diwali celebrations are among the biggest outside India.

Q19660.name: Bucharest
facts: Nicolae Ceaușescu built the Palace of the Parliament, one of the world's largest buildings, here.
Once nicknamed 'Little Paris', it has its own Arc de Triomphe.
Lies on the Dâmbovița River in the plains north of the Danube.

Q17943.name: Arlington
facts: Home of the Dallas Cowboys' AT&T Stadium and baseball's Rangers.
The original Six Flags theme park opened here in 1961.
Lies midway between Dallas and Fort Worth.

Q588.name: Katowice
facts: Its arena, the Spodek, is shaped like a flying saucer.
A coal-mining city, known for the red-brick miners' estate of Nikiszowiec.
Hosts Intel Extreme Masters, one of the biggest esports events, and hosted the 2018 UN climate talks.

Q47164.name: Santa Monica
facts: Its pier marks the western end of Route 66.
The original Muscle Beach started on its sands in the 1930s.
A beach city on the Pacific next to Venice Beach, with a Ferris wheel on the pier.

Q16739.name: Long Beach
facts: The ocean liner Queen Mary is permanently moored here as a hotel.
Its port, beside that of Los Angeles, is one of the busiest container ports in the Americas.
Snoop Dogg grew up here, and an IndyCar Grand Prix races on its streets.

Q1289.name: Grenoble
facts: Hosted the 1968 Winter Olympics.
Bubble-shaped cable cars climb from the centre to the Bastille fortress above.
Called the capital of the Alps, it sits where the Drac meets the Isère; famous for its walnuts.

Q205047.name: Kurdistan Region of Iraq
facts: Its capital is Erbil, whose citadel is one of the oldest inhabited sites in the world.
Its armed forces are the Peshmerga, 'those who face death'.
A mountainous region bordering Turkey, Iran and Syria, home to the Yazidi temple of Lalish.

Q49218.name: Rochester
facts: George Eastman founded Kodak here, and Xerox also grew up here.
Frederick Douglass published his newspaper The North Star here; Susan B. Anthony lived here.
Known as the Flower City, it sits on Lake Ontario where the Genesee River has waterfalls downtown.

Q16959.name: Ürümqi
facts: Said to be the large city farthest from any ocean on Earth.
Sits at the foot of the snowy Tian Shan mountains; the alpine Heavenly Lake is nearby.
A former Silk Road stop with a famous Grand Bazaar.

Q3659.name: N'Djamena
facts: Known as Fort-Lamy until 1973.
Sits where the Chari and Logone rivers meet, facing Kousséri in Cameroon across the water.
Founded by the French in 1900 near the shores of a vast, shrinking lake.

Q3733.name: Conakry
facts: Began on Tombo Island and spread along a narrow peninsula into the Atlantic.
The Îles de Los, a group of islands with beaches, lie just offshore.
Its Grand Mosque is one of the largest in West Africa.

Q2907.name: Sucre
facts: Named after independence hero Antonio José, Bolívar's general; also called the White City.
Independence was declared in 1825 at its Casa de la Libertad.
A nearby cliff, Cal Orck'o, holds thousands of dinosaur footprints.

Q165972.name: Fort Lauderdale
facts: Called the 'Venice of America' for its hundreds of kilometres of canals.
The 1960 film Where the Boys Are made it a spring break hotspot.
Lies on the Atlantic just north of Miami; Port Everglades is a huge cruise port.

Q132754.name: Erbil
facts: Its hilltop citadel is said to be one of the oldest continuously inhabited places on Earth.
Known in ancient times as Arbela; Alexander defeated Darius at Gaugamela nearby.
Also called Hawler, it is the capital of an autonomous region in the north.

Q580.name: Łódź
facts: Its national film school trained Roman Polański, Andrzej Wajda and Krzysztof Kieślowski.
A textile boom town, the setting of Reymont's novel and Wajda's film The Promised Land.
Pianist Arthur Rubinstein was born here; Piotrkowska Street is one of Europe's longest high streets.

Q167715.name: Thiruvananthapuram
facts: The Padmanabhaswamy Temple here was found in 2011 to hold a vast hidden treasure.
The nation's first rocket was launched from nearby Thumba in 1963.
On the Arabian Sea near the subcontinent's southern tip, close to Kovalam beach.

Q184116.name: Gary
facts: The Jackson 5, including Michael Jackson, grew up here.
Founded in 1906 by U.S. Steel and named after the company's chairman, Elbert.
A steel town on the southern shore of Lake Michigan, near Chicago.

Q83813.name: Savannah
facts: Forrest Gump told his life story on a bench in one of its leafy squares.
Laid out in 1733 by James Oglethorpe around a grid of squares; Sherman gave it to Lincoln as a Christmas gift.
The Girl Scouts were founded here by Juliette Gordon Low in 1912.

Q49247.name: Anaheim
facts: Disneyland opened here in 1955.
Its name blends the Santa Ana River with 'heim', German for home, from its founding vintners.
Home of baseball's Angels and hockey's Ducks.

Q25280.name: Harrisburg
facts: The Three Mile Island nuclear accident of 1979 happened just downstream.
Sits on the wide Susquehanna River.
Its domed Capitol was called the 'handsomest building' Theodore Roosevelt had ever seen; Hershey is nearby.

Q79638.name: Fairbanks
facts: One of the best places on Earth to watch the northern lights.
Born in a 1902 gold rush; nicknamed the Golden Heart City.
Winters can drop below -40, yet summer brings near-endless daylight and a midnight baseball game.

Q3881.name: Lusaka
facts: Named after Chief Lusaaka; it replaced Livingstone as capital in 1935.
Its main street is called Cairo Road, after Cecil Rhodes' dream of a Cape-to-Cairo route.
A high plateau city in the south-centre of its landlocked country.

Q4115712.name: Kaunas
facts: Served as the temporary capital between the two world wars.
Japanese diplomat Chiune Sugihara saved thousands of Jews by issuing visas here in 1940.
Sits where the Neris meets the Nemunas, and is mad about basketball and its team Žalgiris.

Q49201.name: Portland
facts: A much-painted lighthouse, the Head Light, guards the entrance to its harbour on Casco Bay.
Poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was born here.
Known for lobster rolls and the cobbled, brick-lined Old Port waterfront.

Q3992.name: Liège
facts: Lies on the River Meuse; Georges Simenon, creator of Inspector Maigret, was born here.
Famous for its chunky, caramelised sugar waffles.
Climb the 374 steps of the Montagne de Bueren; its station was designed by Santiago Calatrava.

Q80985.name: Fez
facts: Al-Qarawiyyin here, founded by Fatima al-Fihri in 859, is often called the oldest university.
Its old walled medina is one of the world's largest car-free urban areas.
Leather is still dyed in honeycomb vats of colour at the Chouara tannery.

Q127856.name: Beverly Hills
facts: Luxury shopping street Rodeo Drive runs through it.
Its ZIP code 90210 became the title of a hit TV drama.
Eddie Murphy's Detroit cop Axel Foley took on its rich and famous in a 1984 film.

Q124739.name: Tijuana
facts: The Caesar salad was invented here in the 1920s by restaurateur Caesar Cardini.
Across the fence from San Diego, it has one of the world's busiest land border crossings.
Avenida Revolución is its famous party street; its football club is the Xolos.

Q9279.name: Bandar Seri Begawan
facts: Kampong Ayer, a huge village of stilt houses built over the river, is part of the city.
The gold-domed Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque overlooks a lagoon here.
The Sultan's Istana Nurul Iman is the world's largest residential palace; it lies on Borneo.

Q48320.name: Kobe
facts: A world-famous marbled beef, from Tajima cattle, bears its name.
Devastated by the Great Hanshin earthquake in 1995.
A port city squeezed between Osaka Bay and the Rokko mountains.

Q187805.name: Spokane
facts: Hosted the 1974 World's Fair on an island beside its roaring river falls.
Father's Day was first celebrated here in 1910, thanks to Sonora Smart Dodd.
Bing Crosby grew up here, and attended Gonzaga, famed for its basketball.

Q485176.name: Pasadena
facts: Hosts the Rose Parade and the Rose Bowl game every New Year's Day.
Home of Caltech and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
The TV sitcom The Big Bang Theory is set here, at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains.

Q49111.name: Cambridge
facts: Home to both Harvard University and MIT.
Lies across the Charles River from Boston.
Matt Damon and Ben Affleck grew up here and set Good Will Hunting around it.

Q163584.name: Derry
facts: Its 17th-century walls are complete, and held out during the Siege of 1689.
Thirteen civil rights marchers were shot dead here on Bloody Sunday in 1972.
Stands on the River Foyle, crossed by a curving Peace Bridge; it throws a huge Halloween festival.

Q393.name: Szczecin
facts: Catherine the Great was born here in 1729 as a minor German princess.
Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' ran from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic.
A port on the Oder River near its lagoon, right by the German border.

Q162442.name: Prayagraj
facts: The Ganges and Yamuna meet here at the sacred Triveni Sangam.
Hosts the Kumbh Mela, the largest gathering of people on Earth.
Home of the Nehru family; Akbar named it Allahabad, its name until 2018.

Q25804.name: Trondheim
facts: Founded by Viking king Olav Tryggvason in 997, and once called Nidaros.
Nidaros Cathedral, built over St Olaf's grave, is the world's northernmost medieval cathedral.
Has a bicycle lift to push cyclists up a steep street; it lies on a long fjord.

Q28271.name: Annapolis
facts: Home of the Naval Academy, on Chesapeake Bay.
Briefly the national capital; Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris here in 1784.
Nicknamed the sailing capital, and known for steamed blue crabs.

Q40840.name: Tampere
facts: Squeezed between two lakes, linked by the Tammerkoski rapids that powered its mills.
Lenin and Stalin first met here in 1905; it has a Lenin museum and a Moomin museum.
Calls itself the sauna capital of the world.

Q38733.name: Helena
facts: Grew from a gold strike at Last Chance Gulch in 1864, now its main street.
Actor Gary Cooper was born here.
The Missouri River cuts through the Gates of the Mountains canyon just north of town.

Q2843.name: Lübeck
facts: The 'Queen of the Hanseatic League', entered through the twin-towered Holstentor gate.
Famous for marzipan, especially from Niederegger.
Thomas Mann set Buddenbrooks here, and Willy Brandt was born here, near the Baltic.

Q2082.name: St. John's
facts: The easternmost city in North America, on the Avalon Peninsula.
Marconi received the first transatlantic radio signal on its Signal Hill in 1901.
Famous for its brightly painted 'Jellybean Row' houses and George Street pubs.

Q1903.name: Catania
facts: Sits at the foot of Mount Etna, Europe's most active volcano.
Rebuilt in Baroque style after the 1693 earthquake; a lava-stone elephant is its symbol.
Composer Vincenzo Bellini was born here; pasta alla Norma is named after his opera.

Q2833.name: Freiburg im Breisgau
facts: Gateway to the Black Forest, near the borders with France and Switzerland.
Little streams called Bächle run through its streets; step in and you'll marry a local, they say.
Known as an eco-city, with the car-free solar suburb Vauban.

Q126084.name: Acre
facts: A crusader capital whose underground Templar tunnel runs under the old city.
Its walls resisted Napoleon's siege in 1799.
On the northern end of Haifa Bay; the holiest Bahá'í shrine is nearby.

Q49225.name: Reno
facts: An arch over its main street calls it 'The Biggest Little City in the World'.
Famous for casinos and, in the 1930s, quick divorces.
Sits on the Truckee River near Lake Tahoe, in the dry rain shadow of the Sierra.

Q2978.name: Regensburg
facts: Its 12th-century Stone Bridge crosses the Danube next to a centuries-old sausage kitchen.
Founded as the Roman fortress Castra Regina.
Its cathedral choir, the Domspatzen, is one of the oldest boys' choirs in the world.

Q5168.name: Makhachkala
facts: A port on the western shore of the Caspian Sea.
Named Port-Petrovsk after Peter the Great, who camped here in 1722.
Renamed in 1921 after the revolutionary Makhach Dakhadayev.

Q49145.name: New Haven
facts: Home of Yale University.
Famous for coal-fired 'apizza', especially from Frank Pepe's; Louis' Lunch claims the first hamburger.
On Long Island Sound; the world's first commercial telephone exchange opened here in 1878.

Q3866.name: Dodoma
facts: Chosen in 1973 to replace Dar es Salaam as capital, though the move took decades.
Its name means 'it has sunk' in the local Gogo language.
The centre of a small wine-growing region in the dry heart of the country.

Q168225.name: Hebron
facts: The Cave of the Patriarchs here is revered as the tomb of Abraham.
Its Arabic name, al-Khalil, means 'the friend', a title of Abraham.
Known for hand-blown glass and grapes, high in the Judean hills.

Q1763.name: Murmansk
facts: The largest city north of the Arctic Circle.
Its port stays ice-free in winter, warmed by the last of the Gulf Stream.
The nuclear icebreaker Lenin is a museum ship here; WWII Arctic convoys sailed to it.

Q8826.name: Palma
facts: Its Gothic cathedral, La Seu, towers over the waterfront and had interior work done by Antoni Gaudí.
It sits on a broad bay on the south coast of Mallorca in the Mediterranean.
Bellver Castle, on a hill above the city, is one of the few circular castles in Europe.

Q1733.name: Magdeburg
facts: The city lies on the Elbe, which a canal crosses here on Europe's longest navigable water bridge.
Mayor Otto von Guericke showed off vacuum power here: teams of horses couldn't pull apart two joined hemispheres.
Emperor Otto the Great is buried in its cathedral.

Q140075.name: Gold Coast
facts: Its beachfront skyline at Surfers Paradise faces the Pacific, about an hour south of Brisbane.
It hosted the 2018 Commonwealth Games.
Theme parks such as Dreamworld, Sea World and Movie World have made it a top holiday spot.

Q20934.name: Incheon
facts: Seoul's main international airport is located here, on reclaimed land on the Yellow Sea.
General MacArthur's daring amphibious landing here in 1950 turned the tide of the Korean War.
Its Chinatown is said to be where the black-bean noodle dish jajangmyeon was born.

Q376749.name: Chittagong
facts: The country's main seaport, it sits on the Bay of Bengal at the mouth of the Karnaphuli River.
Huge ship-breaking yards on the nearby beaches dismantle old ocean liners and tankers by hand.
Muhammad Yunus began the microcredit work behind Grameen Bank in a village by its university.

Q1113311.name: Peshawar
facts: It sits at the eastern end of the Khyber Pass, an ancient gateway to Afghanistan.
Bollywood legends Dilip Kumar and Raj Kapoor were both born here.
Its Qissa Khwani Bazaar is known as the Storytellers' Market, where traders once swapped tales.

Q44564.name: Charleston
facts: It lies where the Elk River meets the Kanawha River in Appalachian hill country.
Its capitol building is crowned by a dome covered in gold leaf.
The public radio music show Mountain Stage is recorded here.

Q72259.name: Portsmouth
facts: Nelson's flagship HMS Victory and Henry VIII's warship the Mary Rose are on display in its historic dockyard.
It's built mostly on Portsea Island, facing the Isle of Wight across the Solent.
Charles Dickens and Isambard Kingdom Brunel were both born here.

Q100188.name: Cluj-Napoca
facts: It is the unofficial capital of the historic region of Transylvania.
Renaissance king Matthias Corvinus was born here, and his statue stands in the main square.
It hosts Untold, one of Europe's biggest electronic music festivals.

Q22690.name: Metz
facts: It sits where the Moselle and Seille rivers meet, close to the borders with Luxembourg and Germany.
Its Gothic cathedral has so much stained glass it's nicknamed the 'Lantern of God'.
A branch of Paris's Centre Pompidou opened here in 2010 under a giant woven, hat-like roof.

Q322.name: Llanfairpwllgwyngyll
facts: Its full 58-letter name is the longest place name in Europe, and its railway station sign is a tourist magnet.
The village is on Anglesey beside the Menai Strait and the Britannia Bridge.
The long version of its name was invented in the 1860s as a publicity stunt to attract visitors.

Q23157.name: Somerset
facts: The Glastonbury Festival takes place here, near the legendary Glastonbury Tor.
Cheddar Gorge gave its name to the world's most popular cheese.
The Georgian spa city of Bath, with its Roman baths, lies within its historic borders.

Q45301.name: Trabzon
facts: The cliff-hugging Sumela Monastery stands in the mountains just inland.
Once called Trebizond, it was capital of a Byzantine splinter empire on the Black Sea coast.
Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent was born here.

Q159260.name: Santa Clara
facts: Levi's Stadium, home of the San Francisco 49ers, is here and hosted Super Bowl 50.
In the heart of Silicon Valley, it is home to the headquarters of Intel and Nvidia.
It grew around a Spanish mission founded in 1777 that now sits on a university campus.

Q28515.name: Springfield
facts: Abraham Lincoln lived and practiced law here, and his tomb is here too.
Historic Route 66 runs through the city.
Its signature dish is the horseshoe: an open sandwich smothered in fries and cheese sauce.

Q28260.name: Lincoln
facts: Originally named Lancaster, it was renamed in 1867 after the recently assassinated president.
Its Cornhuskers football games have sold out Memorial Stadium every game since 1962.
Its tall capitol tower rises above the Great Plains and houses a rare one-house state legislature.

Q9310.name: Dili
facts: A giant Cristo Rei statue stands on a cape overlooking the city's bay.
It lies on the north coast of the island of Timor, which it shares with Indonesia.
It was the capital of a Portuguese colony for centuries until 1975.

Q11959.name: Alicante
facts: Santa Bárbara Castle crowns Mount Benacantil, high above its harbour.
Its palm-lined Explanada promenade is paved with millions of wave-patterned tiles.
Every June it burns huge sculptures in the Hogueras de San Juan bonfire festival.

Q45604.name: Kandahar
facts: It was founded by Alexander the Great, and its name may come from 'Iskandar' (Alexander).
A shrine here holds a cloak said to have belonged to the Prophet Muhammad.
It was the birthplace of the Taliban movement in the 1990s.

Q42622.name: Suzhou
facts: Its classical gardens, such as the Humble Administrator's Garden, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Laced with canals and on the Grand Canal, it's often called the 'Venice of the East'.
It has been famous for its silk and embroidery for centuries.

Q79860.name: Huntsville
facts: Nicknamed 'Rocket City', it's where Wernher von Braun's team built the Saturn V moon rocket.
Space Camp and NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center are both here.
It lies in the north of its state, just north of the Tennessee River.

Q128147.name: Kingston upon Hull
facts: It lies on the north bank of the Humber Estuary, crossed by the Humber Bridge.
Anti-slavery campaigner William Wilberforce was born here.
Its phone boxes are cream rather than red, thanks to its own independent phone company.

Q170322.name: Qingdao
facts: The Tsingtao Brewery was founded here by German settlers in 1903.
It was a German colony until 1914, and red-roofed German buildings survive.
It hosted the sailing events of the 2008 Beijing Olympics on the Yellow Sea.

Q628.name: Bergamo
facts: Its hilltop Città Alta is ringed by Venetian walls that are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Stracciatella gelato was invented here in 1961.
Its football club Atalanta won the Europa League in 2024.

Q49256.name: Bakersfield
facts: Buck Owens and Merle Haggard gave their names to a twangy style of country music born here.
It sits in the oil fields at the southern end of the San Joaquin Valley.
The nu-metal band Korn formed here.

Q185582.name: Knoxville
facts: It hosted the 1982 World's Fair, whose gold Sunsphere tower still stands.
Mountain Dew soda was first created here in the 1940s.
The Great Smoky Mountains rise just to the southeast.

Q3768.name: Yamoussoukro
facts: Its Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, modeled on St Peter's in Rome, is one of the world's largest churches.
It was the home village of founding president Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who made it the capital.
Sacred crocodiles live in the lake beside the presidential palace.

Q49242.name: Corpus Christi
facts: The WWII aircraft carrier USS Lexington is a museum ship on its bayfront.
Padre Island National Seashore, a long barrier island, lies just to the south.
Tejano music star Selena lived here, and a memorial statue honors her on the seawall.

Q159288.name: Santa Barbara
facts: Nicknamed the 'Riviera' of its country, it sits between the Santa Ynez Mountains and the Pacific.
Its Spanish mission is called the 'Queen of the Missions'.
After a 1925 earthquake it was rebuilt in a uniform white-walled, red-tile-roof style.

Q42810.name: Le Havre
facts: Claude Monet painted 'Impression, Sunrise', which named Impressionism, in its harbour.
Rebuilt in concrete by Auguste Perret after WWII, its centre is a UNESCO site.
It sits at the mouth of the Seine on the English Channel, almost on the Prime Meridian.

Q187471.name: Ithaca
facts: In Homer's Odyssey, it is the island home Odysseus spends ten years trying to reach.
It lies in the Ionian Sea, just off the northeast coast of Kefalonia.
Penelope waited here for Odysseus, weaving and unweaving a shroud to fend off suitors.

Q1308.name: Como
facts: It sits at the southern tip of a famous Y-shaped lake beneath the Alps.
Alessandro Volta, inventor of the battery, was born here.
It has long been a centre of silk production.

Q1800.name: Kochi
facts: Its Chinese fishing nets on the waterfront are an iconic sight.
Vasco da Gama was first buried in St Francis Church here before his body went home to Lisbon.
Its airport was the world's first to run fully on solar power.

Q2061.name: Yellowknife
facts: It sits on the north shore of Great Slave Lake, below the Arctic Circle.
It is one of the best places on Earth to watch the northern lights.
It's a base for winter ice roads to remote diamond mines, featured in 'Ice Road Truckers'.

Q40881.name: Carson City
facts: It grew up near the Comstock Lode, and its old mint struck coins from that silver.
Lake Tahoe lies just over the mountains to the west, on the edge of the Sierra Nevada.
It's one of the smaller state capitals, about 30 miles south of Reno.

Q49241.name: Lexington
facts: Known as the 'Horse Capital of the World', it's surrounded by thoroughbred farms.
Keeneland racecourse here is a famous venue for horse racing and sales.
It sits in the heart of the Bluegrass region, close to many bourbon distilleries.

Q25286.name: Uppsala
facts: It has the oldest university in the Nordic countries, founded in 1477.
Botanist Carl Linnaeus taught here, and Anders Celsius was born here.
Royal burial mounds just north of the city mark a great centre of pagan Viking worship.

Q79875.name: Mobile
facts: It celebrated Mardi Gras before New Orleans, starting in the early 1700s.
Admiral Farragut cried 'Damn the torpedoes!' in an 1864 naval battle in its bay.
Baseball legend Hank Aaron was born here.

Q2030.name: Iqaluit
facts: It sits on Frobisher Bay on Baffin Island, and was named Frobisher Bay until 1987.
Its name means 'place of many fish' in Inuktitut.
No road connects it to the rest of the continent; everything arrives by air or by sea.

Q128069.name: Syracuse
facts: It's one of the snowiest big cities in the country, thanks to lake-effect snow off Lake Ontario.
The Erie Canal once ran right through downtown.
It was named after an ancient Greek city in Sicily.

Q1475.name: Quezon City
facts: It was the national capital from 1948 to 1976.
Muhammad Ali beat Joe Frazier in the 'Thrilla in Manila' at its Araneta Coliseum in 1975.
The People Power Monument on EDSA marks the 1986 revolution that toppled Marcos.

Q25923.name: Longyearbyen
facts: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, a 'doomsday' store of crop seeds, is dug into a mountain here.
Polar bears roam nearby, so people carry rifles when they leave town.
Bodies don't decompose in the permafrost, so burials here stopped long ago.

Q169997.name: Darjeeling
facts: It gives its name to a prized black tea grown on the surrounding hills.
A UNESCO-listed narrow-gauge 'toy train' has climbed here since 1881.
On clear days the view is dominated by Kangchenjunga, the world's third-highest mountain.

Q160493.name: Inverness
facts: It sits on the River Ness, at the north end of Loch Ness.
The Battle of Culloden, which crushed the Jacobite rising in 1746, was fought just outside the city.
In Shakespeare's play, King Duncan is murdered at Macbeth's castle here.

Q44254.name: Ushuaia
facts: It calls itself the world's southernmost city, 'the End of the World'.
It sits on the Beagle Channel and is the main departure port for Antarctic cruises.
Its former prison for dangerous convicts is now a museum.

Q919.name: Krasnoyarsk
facts: It lies on the Yenisei, one of the world's great Siberian rivers.
Its bridge and hilltop chapel are pictured on the 10-ruble banknote.
The Stolby nature reserve nearby is famous for its giant granite rock pillars.

Q2119.name: Mannheim
facts: Its centre is a grid of blocks with addresses like 'Q5' or 'N7' instead of street names.
Karl Drais rode the first two-wheeled 'running machine', ancestor of the bicycle, here in 1817.
It lies where the Neckar flows into the Rhine, and its Baroque palace is one of Europe's largest.

Q43382.name: Plymouth
facts: The Pilgrims set sail from here on the Mayflower in 1620.
Legend says Sir Francis Drake finished his game of bowls on the Hoe before fighting the Armada.
It sits between the Plym and Tamar rivers, and is home to a major Royal Navy base.

Q621549.name: Inglewood
facts: SoFi Stadium here hosted Super Bowl LVI in 2022.
Randy's Donuts, with a giant donut on its roof, is a famous landmark next to LAX.
The Forum was the longtime home arena of the Los Angeles Lakers.

Q3955.name: Weimar
facts: Goethe and Schiller both lived and worked here.
The Bauhaus art and design school was founded here in 1919.
In 1919 a national assembly met here to write the democratic constitution after WWI.

Q37133.name: Mariupol
facts: It sits on the northern shore of the Sea of Azov at the mouth of the Kalmius River.
Defenders held out in the vast Azovstal steelworks during the 2022 siege.
Landscape painter Arkhip Kuindzhi was born here.

Q41329.name: Linz
facts: It lies on the Danube, between Vienna and Passau.
A lattice-topped jam tart, one of the oldest known cake recipes, is named after the city.
It hosts Ars Electronica, a famous festival of art, technology and society.

Q170478.name: Bournemouth
facts: Its seven miles of sandy beaches, pier and wooded ravines called 'chines' draw holidaymakers.
Frankenstein author Mary Shelley is buried here, and Tolkien retired here.
Its football club is nicknamed 'the Cherries'.

Q30340.name: Zhengzhou
facts: The Shaolin Temple, birthplace of kung fu, is in its mountains on Mount Song.
It lies near the Yellow River, and was a capital of the ancient Shang dynasty.
A giant Foxconn plant has earned it the nickname 'iPhone City'.

Q11720.name: Shenyang
facts: Under the name Mukden, it has a Qing dynasty imperial palace, smaller sibling of Beijing's.
The 1931 Mukden Incident here was Japan's pretext for invading Manchuria.
The decisive land battle of the 1905 Russo-Japanese War was fought here.

Q3929.name: Port Louis
facts: Its Blue Penny Museum displays some of the world's rarest postage stamps.
Aapravasi Ghat, where indentured labourers from India landed, is a UNESCO site.
Its Champ de Mars racecourse is the oldest in the Southern Hemisphere.

Q3674.name: Niamey
facts: It lies on the banks of the third-longest river in Africa.
Its national museum keeps the remains of the Tree of Ténéré, once the world's most isolated tree.
The last wild West African giraffes roam near Kouré, about an hour away.

Q488004.name: Palm Springs
facts: It's a desert resort in the Coachella Valley, famous for mid-century modern homes.
Frank Sinatra and the Rat Pack made it a Hollywood playground.
A rotating aerial tramway climbs from the desert to the pine forests of Mount San Jacinto.

Q129610.name: Galway
facts: It sits where the River Corrib flows into a bay on the Atlantic coast.
The Claddagh ring, with hands holding a crowned heart, comes from a village here.
The Aran Islands and the wild landscapes of Connemara lie nearby.

Q4191.name: Lucerne
facts: The Chapel Bridge, a 14th-century covered wooden bridge, crosses the Reuss River here.
The Lion Monument, a dying lion carved into a cliff, honors guards killed in Paris in 1792.
Mount Pilatus and the Rigi rise above its lake.

Q4454.name: Khabarovsk
facts: It lies where the Ussuri River joins the Amur, right by the Chinese border.
Its riverside monument to Count Muravyov-Amursky appears on the 5,000-ruble banknote.
It's a major stop on the Trans-Siberian Railway, about 800 km north of Vladivostok.

Q133116.name: Hamilton
facts: The first Tim Hortons doughnut shop opened here in 1964.
Its steel mills earned it the nickname 'Steeltown', and its CFL team is the Tiger-Cats.
With over 100 waterfalls on the Niagara Escarpment, it calls itself the waterfall capital of the world.

Q83317.name: Mosul
facts: It lies on the Tigris, opposite the ruins of ancient Nineveh.
The fine cotton fabric muslin is named after it.
ISIS held it from 2014 to 2017 and blew up its famous leaning al-Hadba minaret.

Q459.name: Plovdiv
facts: It is often called the oldest continuously inhabited city in Europe.
Its Roman theatre, still used for concerts, was discovered after a landslide in the 1970s.
Built on hills, it was once called Philippopolis after Philip II of Macedon.

Q5196.name: Grozny
facts: Its name means 'fearsome' or 'menacing'; it began as an imperial fortress in 1818.
It was largely destroyed in the wars of the 1990s and has been rebuilt with gleaming towers.
It lies on the Sunzha River in the foothills of the Caucasus.

Q133315.name: Limerick
facts: It stands on the River Shannon, guarded by King John's Castle.
Frank McCourt's memoir 'Angela's Ashes' is about growing up poor here.
The rock band The Cranberries formed here.

Q170115.name: Srinagar
facts: Houseboats and shikara boats float on its Dal Lake.
Mughal emperors laid out terraced gardens here, like Shalimar Bagh.
It lies in a Himalayan valley along the Jhelum River.

Q49259.name: Virginia Beach
facts: It's on the Atlantic at the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay, crossed by a famous bridge-tunnel.
The Jamestown colonists first landed at Cape Henry here in 1607.
Music producer and singer Pharrell Williams was born here.

Q25330.name: Trenton
facts: George Washington crossed the icy Delaware River to surprise Hessian troops here in 1776.
A famous bridge sign brags: '... Makes, The World Takes'.
It was briefly the national capital in late 1784.

Q48256.name: Dnipro
facts: It sits on the Dnieper River, from which it takes its current name.
It was first called Yekaterinoslav, 'Glory of Catherine', after Catherine the Great.
It was a secretive centre of Soviet rocket and missile building.

Q2055.name: Whitehorse
facts: It sits on the Alaska Highway, on the river that carried gold-rush stampeders to Dawson City.
Its name comes from foaming rapids said to look like the manes of white horses.
The restored paddlewheeler SS Klondike is beached as a museum in town.

Q279.name: Modena
facts: Enzo Ferrari and Luciano Pavarotti were both born here.
It's the home of traditional balsamic vinegar.
Its Romanesque cathedral and Ghirlandina tower are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Q213205.name: San Francisco Bay Area
facts: The Golden Gate Bridge spans the strait into its bay.
Silicon Valley, home of Apple, Google and Stanford, lies at its southern end.
The San Andreas Fault runs through it, and the 1906 earthquake devastated the area.

Q92561.name: London
facts: It sits on its own Thames River and has streets named after those in its English namesake.
Actors Ryan Gosling and Rachel McAdams were both born here.
The Labatt brewery was founded here in 1847.

Q68097.name: Davos
facts: World leaders and CEOs gather here every January for the World Economic Forum.
Thomas Mann set his novel 'The Magic Mountain' in a tuberculosis sanatorium here.
It hosts the Spengler Cup, one of the oldest ice hockey tournaments, every December.

Q1721.name: Wiesbaden
facts: Its hot springs have made it a spa town since Roman times.
Dostoevsky gambled away money at its casino, inspiring his novel 'The Gambler'.
It lies on the Rhine opposite Mainz, below the Taunus hills.

Q39561.name: Burbank
facts: Warner Bros. and Disney have studios here, earning it the title 'Media Capital of the World'.
Johnny Carson's 'Tonight Show' was taped here for decades.
Director Tim Burton was born here.

Q34109.name: Fargo
facts: A 1996 Coen brothers film and later TV series borrowed its name.
It sits on the Red River of the North, facing Moorhead, Minnesota.
It sits on the flat prairie and is known for long, bitterly cold winters and big river floods.

Q184587.name: Grand Rapids
facts: Nicknamed 'Furniture City', it was once the country's furniture-making capital.
President Gerald Ford grew up here, and his presidential museum and grave are here.
It became the first city in the world to fluoridate its drinking water, in 1945.

Q139564.name: Atlantic City
facts: Its streets inspired the property names on the original Monopoly board.
Its famous oceanfront Boardwalk, opened in 1870, was the first of its kind in the country.
The Miss America pageant was born here in 1921.

Q130191.name: Norwich
facts: Colman's mustard was made here for nearly two centuries.
Its Norman cathedral has one of the tallest spires in the country.
Its football club, the Canaries, is part-owned by TV cook Delia Smith.

Q49236.name: St. Petersburg
facts: The Salvador Dalí Museum holds one of the world's largest Dalí collections.
The world's first scheduled commercial airline flight left here for Tampa in 1914.
Nicknamed the 'Sunshine City', it is linked south by the soaring Sunshine Skyway Bridge.

Q10566.name: Saskatoon
facts: It's named after a sweet purple prairie berry.
Joni Mitchell and hockey great Gordie Howe both grew up here.
Nicknamed 'Bridge City', it is crossed by many bridges over its river.

Q23051.name: Swansea
facts: Poet Dylan Thomas was born here and called it an 'ugly, lovely town'.
The Gower Peninsula next door was the first place to be named an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
Catherine Zeta-Jones grew up here.

Q430464.name: Dearborn
facts: Henry Ford was born here, and the Ford Motor Company has its headquarters here.
The Henry Ford museum and Greenfield Village are in the city.
It has one of the country's largest Arab communities, and is Ford's hometown.

Q42735.name: Olympia
facts: It sits at the southern tip of Puget Sound, with views of the Olympic Mountains.
It's a birthplace of the 1990s riot grrrl punk movement, including Bikini Kill.
Its old brewery sold beer with the slogan 'It's the Water'.

Q183113.name: Bora Bora
facts: The island's lagoon is ringed by a barrier reef around the peak of Mount Otemanu.
It's famous for luxury overwater bungalows on its turquoise lagoon.
In WWII the US used it as a supply base; old cannons still dot the island.

Q131335.name: Sioux Falls
facts: Its downtown Falls Park has waterfalls tumbling over pink quartzite rock.
Citibank and others moved credit card operations here after the state scrapped interest-rate caps.
It sits near where its state meets Minnesota and Iowa.

Q1707.name: Kiel
facts: Each June it hosts one of the world's largest sailing festivals, and it hosted Olympic sailing twice.
The world's busiest artificial waterway, linking the North Sea to the Baltic, ends here.
A sailors' mutiny here in 1918 sparked the revolution that ended the Kaiser's reign.

Q52028.name: Chiang Mai
facts: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep, a golden temple, looks down on the city from a mountain.
Thousands of paper lanterns float into the sky here during the Yi Peng festival.
Founded by King Mangrai in 1296, it was capital of the Lanna Kingdom; its old city is ringed by a moat.

Q7003.name: Dijon
facts: It gave its name to a famous smooth, strong mustard.
Gustave Eiffel, of Eiffel Tower fame, was born here.
Visitors rub a small stone owl on the Notre-Dame church for good luck.

Q38511.name: Turku
facts: It is the country's oldest city and was its capital until 1812.
It sits at the mouth of the Aura River, facing a vast archipelago.
Each Christmas Eve a medieval Declaration of Christmas Peace is read out here.

Q200016.name: Visakhapatnam
facts: It sits between the Eastern Ghats hills and the Bay of Bengal.
A real submarine, INS Kursura, is displayed as a museum on its Ramakrishna Beach.
It is home to the navy's Eastern Naval Command, the main base on the Bay of Bengal.

Q26339.name: Jersey City
facts: It faces Lower Manhattan across the Hudson River.
Liberty State Park here has close-up views of the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island.
The giant Colgate Clock on its waterfront once marked the toothpaste company's factory.

Q13666.name: Messina
facts: It faces Calabria across a narrow strait, home of the mythical Scylla and Charybdis.
Its cathedral bell tower has one of the world's largest astronomical clocks.
It was devastated by an earthquake and tsunami in 1908.

Q1309.name: Maastricht
facts: The 1992 treaty that created the European Union was signed here.
It straddles the Meuse River, wedged between Belgium and Germany.
One of its bookshops is set inside a 13th-century Dominican church.

Q62823.name: Barranquilla
facts: Its Carnival is the country's biggest and is recognised by UNESCO.
Singer Shakira and actress Sofía Vergara were both born here.
It sits near where the Magdalena River meets the Caribbean Sea.

Q43509.name: Guayaquil
facts: It lies on the Guayas River, with a long riverfront promenade called the Malecón 2000.
Land iguanas roam freely in its downtown Parque Seminario.
It's a main gateway for flights to the Galápagos Islands.

Q911.name: Ufa
facts: It sits on hills where two rivers meet the Belaya, on the western side of the southern Urals.
Ballet star Rudolf Nureyev grew up here.
A huge equestrian statue of the folk hero Salawat Yulayev overlooks the river.

Q204234.name: Milton Keynes
facts: It's famous for its concrete cows sculpture and its many roundabouts.
A 1960s planned new town, it's laid out on a grid of fast roads.
Bletchley Park, where WWII codebreakers cracked Enigma, is in the city.

Q49239.name: Toledo
facts: Sits at the western tip of Lake Erie where the Maumee River flows in.
Nicknamed the Glass City for its long history of glassmaking companies like Libbey and Owens-Corning.
Jeeps have been built here since the 1940s, and its minor-league baseball team is the quirky Mud Hens.

Q908.name: Rostov-on-Don
facts: Lies on the Don River about 30 km before it reaches the Sea of Azov.
Long called the Gateway to the Caucasus, the mountain region lying to its south.
Hosted matches of the 2018 FIFA World Cup at a new riverside stadium.

Q48344.name: Recife
facts: Its name means 'reef', after the long coral reefs that shelter its Atlantic beaches.
Crisscrossed by rivers and bridges, it is often compared to Venice.
Famous for frenetic frevo dancing at Carnival, shared with the hilltop colonial town of Olinda next door.

Q199797.name: Tacoma
facts: A port city on Puget Sound, about 50 km south of Seattle.
Its first Narrows Bridge, 'Galloping Gertie', twisted wildly and collapsed in the wind in 1940.
Glass artist Dale Chihuly was born here, and it now has a Museum of Glass.

Q170573.name: Qom
facts: One of Shia Islam's holiest cities, home to the gold-domed shrine of Fatima Masumeh.
Its huge religious seminaries trained many clerics, including Ayatollah Khomeini.
Lies about 140 km south of Tehran, on the edge of a vast salt desert.

Q79809.name: Utqiagvik
facts: The northernmost city of its country, on the Arctic Ocean shore near Point Barrow.
The sun does not rise for about two months each winter and does not set for about 80 days in summer.
Inupiat whaling town where humorist Will Rogers and aviator Wiley Post died in a 1935 plane crash nearby.

Q25319.name: Aarhus
facts: Sits on the east coast of the Jutland peninsula, facing the Kattegat sea.
Its ARoS art museum is topped by a circular rainbow-coloured glass walkway.
Den Gamle By, an open-air museum of historic town houses, recreates life in centuries past.

Q2123.name: Regina
facts: Its original name was Pile o' Bones, after a heap of bison bones left by hunters.
Home of the Mounties' national training academy for new police recruits.
Fans of its CFL team, the Roughriders, famously wear hollowed-out watermelons on their heads.

Q487988.name: St. Augustine
facts: Founded by the Spanish in 1565, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in its country.
Guarded by the Castillo de San Marcos, a 17th-century stone fort made of coquina shell rock.
Legend links it to Ponce de Leon's search for the Fountain of Youth, now a tourist park.

Q163132.name: Akron
facts: Once the Rubber Capital of the World, home to Goodyear and Firestone tyre makers.
Basketball superstar LeBron James was born and raised here.
Alcoholics Anonymous was founded here in 1935.

Q41057.name: Topeka
facts: Its school segregation case, Brown v. Board of Education, ended legal school segregation nationwide in 1954.
Sits on the Kaw River in the middle of the Great Plains.
Charles Curtis, the first vice president of Native American ancestry, was born here.

Q166304.name: Billings
facts: Sits on the Yellowstone River beneath tall sandstone cliffs called the Rimrocks.
Nearby Pompeys Pillar bears William Clark's carved signature from the Lewis and Clark expedition.
The Little Bighorn battlefield, site of Custer's Last Stand, lies to its southeast.

Q49231.name: Norfolk
facts: Home to the world's largest naval base, headquarters of the Atlantic Fleet.
Sits on Hampton Roads where the James and Elizabeth rivers meet the Chesapeake Bay.
General Douglas MacArthur is buried here, and the battleship USS Wisconsin is moored downtown as a museum.

Q28237.name: Lansing
facts: Ransom Olds founded the Oldsmobile car company here in the 1890s.
Basketball star Magic Johnson was born and grew up here.
Lies where the Red Cedar River joins the Grand River, next door to the Spartans' university campus.

Q48403.name: Amritsar
facts: Home of the Golden Temple, Harmandir Sahib, the holiest shrine of Sikhism.
Site of the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre by British troops.
Near the Wagah border, famous for its daily flag-lowering ceremony with Pakistan.

Q189288.name: Stratford-upon-Avon
facts: William Shakespeare was born here in 1564 and is buried in its Holy Trinity Church.
Home of the Royal Shakespeare Company and its riverside theatres.
Anne Hathaway's thatched cottage, home of Shakespeare's wife, is on its outskirts.

Q186702.name: Chattanooga
facts: Glenn Miller's 1941 big-band hit about a 'Choo Choo' train made its name famous.
Overlooked by Lookout Mountain, home to Rock City and the underground waterfall Ruby Falls.
Coca-Cola was first bottled here in 1899, under the world's first bottling franchise.

Q484678.name: Berkeley
facts: Its university campus launched the Free Speech Movement of 1964.
The elements berkelium and californium were discovered in its labs.
Sits on the east shore of San Francisco Bay, facing the Golden Gate; Alice Waters' Chez Panisse is here.

Q38807.name: Suva
facts: Lies on the southeast coast of Viti Levu island in the South Pacific.
Main campus of the University of the South Pacific, shared by a dozen island nations.
Replaced Levuka as the colonial capital in 1877, partly for its better harbour.

Q898.name: Omsk
facts: Sits where the Om River meets the Irtysh in southwestern Siberia.
Dostoevsky spent four years in its prison camp, inspiring his book The House of the Dead.
Served as the capital of Admiral Kolchak's White government during the Civil War.

Q1040.name: Karlsruhe
facts: Its streets fan out from the palace like the ribs of a fan, giving it the nickname Fan City.
Seat of the country's Federal Constitutional Court and Federal Court of Justice.
Car pioneer Carl Benz and bicycle-forerunner inventor Karl Drais were both born here.

Q485708.name: Duluth
facts: Sits at the far western tip of Lake Superior, a busy port for iron-ore freighters.
Its Aerial Lift Bridge raises its whole deck to let ships into the harbour.
Bob Dylan was born here in 1941.

Q80989.name: Bhopal
facts: Site of the 1984 Union Carbide gas leak, one of the worst industrial disasters ever.
Known as the City of Lakes, built around the large Upper Lake, Bhojtal.
The ancient Buddhist stupa of Sanchi lies a short drive to the northeast.

Q43919.name: Salem
facts: Sits on the Willamette River in the heart of the Willamette Valley.
Its capitol is topped by a gilded statue of a pioneer with an axe.
Willamette University here, founded in 1842, is the oldest university in the West.

Q39984.name: Cannes
facts: Hosts the world's most famous film festival, where the Palme d'Or is awarded.
Its palm-lined seafront promenade is La Croisette, on the Mediterranean west of Nice.
The Man in the Iron Mask was imprisoned on Sainte-Marguerite, one of the Lerins Islands just offshore.

Q47430.name: Green Bay
facts: Home of the Packers, the only community-owned team in the NFL, at Lambeau Field.
Its football success earned it the nickname Titletown; fans wear foam cheesehead hats.
Lies at the mouth of the Fox River on an arm of Lake Michigan.

Q2066.name: Essen
facts: The Zollverein coal mine, a Bauhaus-style industrial complex, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Long the base of the Krupp steel and arms dynasty, in the heart of the Ruhr.
The Albrecht brothers founded the Aldi supermarket chain here.

Q17872.name: Alice Springs
facts: Sits near the very centre of its continent, beside the MacDonnell Ranges.
Hosts the Henley-on-Todd Regatta, a boat race held on a dry riverbed with bottomless boats.
Base of the School of the Air, which taught outback children by radio, and the Flying Doctor service.

Q175517.name: Norilsk
facts: One of the world's northernmost cities, far above the Arctic Circle in Siberia.
Built by Gulag prisoners to mine vast deposits of nickel and palladium.
A closed city where foreigners need special permission to visit.

Q31058.name: Burlington
facts: Sits on the shore of Lake Champlain, facing the Adirondack Mountains.
Ben & Jerry's ice cream began here in 1978 in a converted gas station.
Bernie Sanders was its mayor in the 1980s, and the band Phish formed here.

Q485172.name: Ann Arbor
facts: Its university's football stadium, The Big House, is the largest stadium in the Americas.
The Borders bookstore chain began here, and it hosts a huge annual summer art fair.
Gerald Ford's presidential library stands on its university campus by the Huron River.

Q161491.name: Reading
facts: Sits where the River Kennet joins the Thames, west of London.
Oscar Wilde was imprisoned in its gaol, inspiring his famous ballad.
Hosts a huge annual rock festival every August bank holiday, twinned with Leeds.

Q37066.name: Bismarck
facts: Sits on the east bank of the Missouri River, which Lewis and Clark travelled.
Its Art Deco capitol tower is nicknamed the Skyscraper of the Prairie.
Custer set out for the Little Bighorn from nearby Fort Abraham Lincoln in 1876.

Q2999.name: Würzburg
facts: Its Residence palace boasts one of the world's largest ceiling frescoes, painted by Tiepolo.
Wilhelm Rontgen discovered X-rays here in 1895.
Lies on the Main River, surrounded by vineyards known for wine in flat, round Bocksbeutel bottles.

Q2235.name: Veliky Novgorod
facts: One of the oldest cities of the Rus', on the Volkhov River near Lake Ilmen.
Archaeologists have dug up over a thousand medieval letters written on birch bark here.
Its kremlin holds a giant bronze monument to 1,000 years of the nation since Rurik in 862.

Q387047.name: Malibu
facts: A string of beaches along the Pacific Coast Highway, beneath the Santa Monica Mountains.
Surfrider Beach here was a birthplace of 1950s-60s surf culture.
Home to the Getty Villa, a replica Roman country house full of ancient art.

Q188304.name: Sunderland
facts: Sits at the mouth of the River Wear on the North Sea coast.
Once billed as the largest shipbuilding town in the world.
Its football club, the Black Cats, plays at the Stadium of Light.

Q40269.name: Porto Alegre
facts: Lies on the shore of Lake Guaiba in the far south, close to Uruguay.
Hosted the first World Social Forum in 2001.
Home to the fierce football rivals Gremio and Internacional, and to gaucho churrasco and chimarrao tea.

Q49243.name: Riverside
facts: Named for the Santa Ana River beside it, east of Los Angeles.
The parent navel orange tree, planted in 1873, still grows here and sparked the citrus boom.
Famed for the Mission Inn, a sprawling Mission Revival hotel where presidents stayed.

Q9832.name: Eindhoven
facts: The electronics giant Philips was founded here in 1891.
Its football club PSV was founded by Philips as a works team.
Nicknamed the City of Light and known for its annual Design Week and tech hub Brainport.

Q3799.name: Porto-Novo
facts: The official capital, though nearby Cotonou is the real seat of government.
Sits on a lagoon near the Gulf of Guinea coast, close to the border with Nigeria.
Founded as Hogbonu, it was a Portuguese slave-trade port; its Great Mosque echoes Afro-Brazilian church design.

Q174224.name: Wilmington
facts: The DuPont company began here in 1802 as a gunpowder mill on Brandywine Creek.
Joe Biden's longtime hometown; its train station is named after him.
Lies on the Christina River, about 50 km southwest of Philadelphia.

Q6526.name: Bolzano
facts: Its archaeology museum displays Otzi the Iceman, a 5,300-year-old mummy found in the Alps.
A gateway to the Dolomites, on the road to the Brenner Pass.
Officially bilingual, with German and Italian names, and known for its Christmas market.

Q172157.name: Winchester
facts: The ancient capital of King Alfred the Great's kingdom of Wessex.
Jane Austen is buried in its cathedral, which has one of the longest naves in Europe.
A legendary 'Round Table of King Arthur' hangs in its Great Hall.

Q3726.name: Banjul
facts: Sits on St Mary's Island where a great river meets the Atlantic.
Was called Bathurst until 1973.
Entered through Arch 22, a huge gateway monument built to mark a 1994 coup.

Q54140.name: Salem
facts: Infamous for the 1692 witch trials, which led to 20 executions.
Nathaniel Hawthorne was born here and set The House of the Seven Gables in town.
Draws huge crowds every October for a month-long Halloween festival.

Q171866.name: Middlesbrough
facts: Its Tees Transporter Bridge carries cars across the River Tees in a hanging gondola.
Home of the parmo, a breaded cutlet smothered in bechamel and cheese.
Captain James Cook was born in Marton, now part of the town.

Q123709.name: Dundee
facts: Famous for the three Js: jute, jam and journalism.
The Beano and The Dandy comics were published here, and Scott's ship RRS Discovery is moored here.
Sits on the north bank of the Firth of Tay; the Tay Bridge collapsed under a train in 1879.

Q160544.name: Heraklion
